/glossary.t: No-Win-No-Fee Glossary: CFA, DBA, Contingency Fee, Cuota Litis
/glossary.d: Plain-language definitions of no-win-no-fee terms: contingency fee, CFA, DBA, ATE insurance, litigation funding, cuota litis, Erfolgshonorar and more…

faq.q: What is No win, no fee?
faq.a: An arrangement where you do not pay your own lawyer's fees if the case is lost. If you win, the lawyer is paid from the result or recovers fees from the other side. Court fees, expert costs and the other side's costs may still apply, so read the agreement.

faq.q: What is Contingency fee?
faq.a: The lawyer's fee is a percentage of the money recovered and nothing is due if there is no recovery. The percentage, and whether expenses are deducted before or after it, is set in the written agreement and is limited by local rules in some places.

faq.q: What is Conditional fee agreement (CFA)?
faq.a: The lawyer charges normal fees only if you win, plus a success fee on top of those fees. The success fee cannot exceed 100% of the base costs, and in personal injury claims it is capped at 25% of certain damages.

faq.q: What is Damages-based agreement (DBA)?
faq.a: The lawyer takes a percentage of the damages you recover instead of hourly fees. The cap, including VAT, is 25% in personal injury claims, 35% in employment claims and 50% in other claims.

faq.q: What is After-the-event (ATE) insurance?
faq.a: Insurance bought after a dispute arises that pays the other side's costs, and often your own expenses, if you lose. The premium is frequently deferred and payable only if you win.

faq.q: What is Adverse costs (loser pays)?
faq.a: The rule that the losing party pays part of the winner's legal costs. It is why a no-win-no-fee agreement with your own lawyer does not always mean you risk nothing.

faq.q: What is Litigation funding (third-party funding)?
faq.a: A company that is not a party to the case pays the legal costs in exchange for a share of the money recovered. Funding is usually non-recourse: if the case is lost, you do not repay the funder.

faq.q: What is Cuota litis?
faq.a: An agreement where the lawyer's fee depends on the result, usually a percentage of what is obtained. In Spain the professional ban on it was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2008, so it can be agreed freely in writing.

faq.q: What is Patto di quota lite?
faq.a: An agreement giving the lawyer a share of the asset or sum in dispute. Since 2012 Italian law forbids it again, but a fee calculated as a percentage of the value of the case, agreed in writing in advance, is allowed.

faq.q: What is Erfolgshonorar?
faq.a: A fee that depends on success. It is generally not allowed for lawyers, with exceptions: for example claims of up to 2,000 euros, certain debt collection work, and cases where the client could not otherwise afford to bring the claim.

faq.q: What is Honoraire de résultat?
faq.a: A bonus linked to the result. A fee based only on the result (pacte de quota litis) is not allowed, but a result-based fee can be added to a fixed or hourly fee if it is agreed in writing.

faq.q: What is Success fee?
faq.a: Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.

faq.q: What is Limitation period?
faq.a: The deadline for starting a claim. Once it has passed the claim is usually barred, so check it early; periods differ by country and type of claim and can be paused or restarted in some situations.

faq.q: What is Legal expenses insurance (BTE)?
faq.a: Insurance bought before any dispute arises ("before the event"), often included in home, car or bank policies, that pays legal costs if a covered dispute comes up. Check your policies before agreeing anything else: the insurer may have to approve the lawyer and the costs.

faq.q: What is Qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS)?
faq.a: A rule for most personal injury claims under which a claimant who loses is generally not ordered to pay the defendant's costs out of their own pocket. Costs orders can still be set off against damages, and the protection can be lost, for example if the claim is found to be fundamentally dishonest.

faq.q: What is Disbursements?
faq.a: Expenses a lawyer pays to third parties while running your case, such as court fees, expert reports, medical records and translations. Some no-win-no-fee agreements cover them if you lose; others make you pay them whatever the result. The agreement should say which.

faq.q: What is Class action?
faq.a: A single case brought by one or more representatives on behalf of a larger group with similar claims. Members are often included unless they opt out, and any settlement usually needs the court's approval. Lawyers in class actions are frequently paid on a contingency basis.

faq.q: What is EU representative action?
faq.a: A collective action brought by an approved organisation (a "qualified entity") on behalf of consumers, under Directive (EU) 2020/1828, to stop an unlawful practice or obtain redress. Each member state sets its own details, including whether consumers opt in or opt out.

faq.q: What is Group litigation order (GLO)?
faq.a: A court order that manages many separate claims raising common issues together. Claimants usually join by being entered on a group register, and decisions on the common issues bind the claims on the register.

faq.q: What is Letter before action?
faq.a: A formal letter to the other side setting out the claim, what you want and a deadline to respond, sent before starting court proceedings. Courts expect it, and skipping it can affect who pays the costs. Our free claim letter tool helps you draft one.

faq.q: What is Statute of limitations?
faq.a: The US name for the law that sets the deadline for filing a lawsuit. Each state sets its own periods by type of claim, and federal claims have their own, so the same claim can have different deadlines in different states.

faq.q: What is Small claims procedure?
faq.a: A simpler and cheaper court procedure for low-value claims, designed so that people can bring a claim without a lawyer. The value limit and the costs rules differ by country; in England and Wales the small claims track generally covers claims up to £10,000.

faq.q: What is Out-of-court settlement?
faq.a: An agreement that ends a dispute without a court judgment, usually in exchange for a payment. Most claims settle. On a no-win-no-fee agreement, a settlement normally counts as a win, so the lawyer's success fee or percentage applies to the amount agreed.

faq.q: What is Burofax?
faq.a: A certified communication sent through the Spanish postal service with proof of content and delivery. It is commonly used to send a formal demand before a claim, and a demand received by the debtor can interrupt the limitation period.

faq.q: What is Proceso monitorio?
faq.a: A fast Spanish court procedure to recover a money debt backed by documents, such as invoices or a signed contract. The initial application can be filed without a lawyer. If the debtor does not pay or object, the court can order enforcement.

faq.q: What is European order for payment?
faq.a: A procedure under Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 to recover uncontested money claims across EU borders using standard forms. If the debtor does not object, the order becomes enforceable in the other member states.

faq.q: What is European Small Claims Procedure?
faq.a: A written procedure for cross-border claims of up to €5,000 under Regulation (EC) No 861/2007, using standard forms and usually without a hearing. A lawyer is not required.

faq.q: What is Funding multiple?
faq.a: A way of setting a litigation funder's return as a multiple of the money it invests in the case, often compared with, or combined with, a percentage of the recovery. The funding agreement should state how the return is calculated and in what order the proceeds are paid out.

faq.q: What is Non-recourse funding?
faq.a: Funding that is repaid only out of what the case recovers. If the case is lost, you owe the funder nothing. Most third-party litigation funding works this way, but check whether the agreement also covers the other side's costs.

faq.q: What is Security for costs?
faq.a: An order requiring a claimant to pay money into court or give a guarantee to cover the defendant's costs if the claim fails, for example when the claimant lives abroad or is a company that may not be able to pay. Funders and ATE insurers can sometimes provide it.

faq.q: What is Pactum de quota litis?
faq.a: Latin for an agreement under which a lawyer's fee is only a share of what the client wins. Many civil-law countries forbid it while allowing a success bonus on top of a base fee; Spain has allowed it since 2008.

faq.q: What is Honorários de êxito?
faq.a: A success fee agreed between client and lawyer, often alongside a smaller fixed fee. It is separate from the honorários de sucumbência, the costs a court orders the losing side to pay to the winner's lawyer.

faq.q: What is Prozessfinanzierung?
faq.a: The German term for third-party litigation funding: a funder pays the court and lawyer costs, and the other side's costs if the case is lost, in return for a share of the proceeds agreed in the contract. Funders usually look for larger claims with good prospects.

faq.q: What is No foil, no fee?
faq.a: The Irish form of no-win-no-fee: the solicitor charges no fee if the case is lost. Irish solicitors may not charge a percentage of the damages, and you may still face the other side's costs if you lose.

faq.q: What is Claims management company (CMC)?
faq.a: A business that handles claims for a share of the compensation, often passing them to a law firm. In Great Britain, CMCs have been regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority since 2019. Many claims can be made directly for free, so check before signing.

faq.q: What is Costs follow the event?
faq.a: The general principle that the losing party pays the winning party's legal costs, usually only part of them, as assessed by the court. Courts can depart from it, for example when the winner behaved unreasonably.

faq.q: What is American rule on costs?
faq.a: The principle that each side pays its own lawyer whatever the result, unless a statute or contract says otherwise. It is one reason contingency fees work well in the US: losing usually does not mean paying the other side's lawyer.

faq.q: What is Disclosure of documents?
faq.a: The stage of a case in which each side must reveal relevant documents, including some that harm its own case. It can be costly and time-consuming, which is one reason lawyers and funders weigh it when deciding whether to take a case.

faq.q: What is Late payment interest?
faq.a: Statutory interest a business can charge on late payment by another business. Under the EU Late Payment Directive the rate is at least 8 percentage points above the reference rate, plus a fixed €40 compensation per invoice; the UK has its own similar rules. Our free calculator works it out.

faq.q: What is EU261 flight compensation?
faq.a: Fixed compensation under Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 of €250, €400 or €600 depending on flight distance, for long delays at arrival, late cancellations and denied boarding, unless the airline proves extraordinary circumstances. The UK version pays similar amounts in pounds.

/glossary/erfolgshonorar.lead: A fee that depends on success. It is generally not allowed for lawyers, with exceptions: for example claims of up to 2,000 euros, certain debt collection work, and cases where the client could not otherwise afford to bring the claim.

faq.q: What is Erfolgshonorar?
faq.a: A fee that depends on success. It is generally not allowed for lawyers, with exceptions: for example claims of up to 2,000 euros, certain debt collection work, and cases where the client could not otherwise afford to bring the claim.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in Germany.

/glossary/honoraire-de-resultat.t: Honoraire de résultat: Meaning and How It Works

/glossary/honoraire-de-resultat.lead: A bonus linked to the result. A fee based only on the result (pacte de quota litis) is not allowed, but a result-based fee can be added to a fixed or hourly fee if it is agreed in writing.

faq.q: What is Honoraire de résultat?
faq.a: A bonus linked to the result. A fee based only on the result (pacte de quota litis) is not allowed, but a result-based fee can be added to a fixed or hourly fee if it is agreed in writing.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in France.

/glossary/success-fee.t: Success fee: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/success-fee.d: Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.
/glossary/success-fee.lead: Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.

faq.q: What is Success fee?
faq.a: Any fee, or part of a fee, that is payable only if the case succeeds. How it is calculated, and whether it is allowed at all, depends on the country.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: It is a general term, used in many countries.

/glossary/limitation-period.t: Limitation period: Meaning and How It Works

/glossary/limitation-period.lead: The deadline for starting a claim. Once it has passed the claim is usually barred, so check it early; periods differ by country and type of claim and can be paused or restarted in some situations.

faq.q: What is Limitation period?
faq.a: The deadline for starting a claim. Once it has passed the claim is usually barred, so check it early; periods differ by country and type of claim and can be paused or restarted in some situations.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: It is a general term, used in many countries.

/glossary/legal-expenses-insurance.t: Legal expenses insurance (BTE): Meaning and How It Works

/glossary/legal-expenses-insurance.lead: Insurance bought before any dispute arises ("before the event"), often included in home, car or bank policies, that pays legal costs if a covered dispute comes up. Check your policies before agreeing anything else: the insurer may have to approve the lawyer and the costs.

faq.q: What is Legal expenses insurance?
faq.a: Insurance bought before any dispute arises ("before the event"), often included in home, car or bank policies, that pays legal costs if a covered dispute comes up. Check your policies before agreeing anything else: the insurer may have to approve the lawyer and the costs.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in General, common in Germany, Austria, Scandinavia and the UK.

/glossary/qualified-one-way-costs-shifti.t: Qualified one-way costs shifting (QOCS): Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/qualified-one-way-costs-shifti.d: A rule for most personal injury claims under which a claimant who loses is generally not ordered to pay the defendant's costs out of their own pocket.
/glossary/qualified-one-way-costs-shifti.lead: A rule for most personal injury claims under which a claimant who loses is generally not ordered to pay the defendant's costs out of their own pocket. Costs orders can still be set off against damages, and the protection can be lost, for example if the claim is found to be fundamentally dishonest.

faq.q: What is Qualified one-way costs shifting?
faq.a: A rule for most personal injury claims under which a claimant who loses is generally not ordered to pay the defendant's costs out of their own pocket. Costs orders can still be set off against damages, and the protection can be lost, for example if the claim is found to be fundamentally dishonest.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in England and Wales.

/glossary/disbursements.t: Disbursements: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/disbursements.d: Expenses a lawyer pays to third parties while running your case, such as court fees, expert reports, medical records and translations.
/glossary/disbursements.lead: Expenses a lawyer pays to third parties while running your case, such as court fees, expert reports, medical records and translations. Some no-win-no-fee agreements cover them if you lose; others make you pay them whatever the result. The agreement should say which.

faq.q: What is Disbursements?
faq.a: Expenses a lawyer pays to third parties while running your case, such as court fees, expert reports, medical records and translations. Some no-win-no-fee agreements cover them if you lose; others make you pay them whatever the result. The agreement should say which.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: It is a general term, used in many countries.

/glossary/class-action.t: Class action: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/class-action.d: A single case brought by one or more representatives on behalf of a larger group with similar claims. Members are often included unless they opt out, and…
/glossary/class-action.lead: A single case brought by one or more representatives on behalf of a larger group with similar claims. Members are often included unless they opt out, and any settlement usually needs the court's approval. Lawyers in class actions are frequently paid on a contingency basis.

faq.q: What is Class action?
faq.a: A single case brought by one or more representatives on behalf of a larger group with similar claims. Members are often included unless they opt out, and any settlement usually needs the court's approval. Lawyers in class actions are frequently paid on a contingency basis.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in United States, Canada, Australia and others.

/glossary/eu-representative-action.t: EU representative action: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/eu-representative-action.d: A collective action brought by an approved organisation (a "qualified entity") on behalf of consumers, under Directive (EU) 2020/1828, to stop an unlawful…
/glossary/eu-representative-action.lead: A collective action brought by an approved organisation (a "qualified entity") on behalf of consumers, under Directive (EU) 2020/1828, to stop an unlawful practice or obtain redress. Each member state sets its own details, including whether consumers opt in or opt out.

faq.q: What is EU representative action?
faq.a: A collective action brought by an approved organisation (a "qualified entity") on behalf of consumers, under Directive (EU) 2020/1828, to stop an unlawful practice or obtain redress. Each member state sets its own details, including whether consumers opt in or opt out.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in European Union.

/glossary/group-litigation-order.t: Group litigation order (GLO): Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/group-litigation-order.d: A court order that manages many separate claims raising common issues together. Claimants usually join by being entered on a group register, and decisions…
/glossary/group-litigation-order.lead: A court order that manages many separate claims raising common issues together. Claimants usually join by being entered on a group register, and decisions on the common issues bind the claims on the register.

faq.q: What is Group litigation order?
faq.a: A court order that manages many separate claims raising common issues together. Claimants usually join by being entered on a group register, and decisions on the common issues bind the claims on the register.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in England and Wales.

/glossary/letter-before-action.t: Letter before action: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/letter-before-action.d: A formal letter to the other side setting out the claim, what you want and a deadline to respond, sent before starting court proceedings.
/glossary/letter-before-action.lead: A formal letter to the other side setting out the claim, what you want and a deadline to respond, sent before starting court proceedings. Courts expect it, and skipping it can affect who pays the costs. Our free claim letter tool helps you draft one.

faq.q: What is Letter before action?
faq.a: A formal letter to the other side setting out the claim, what you want and a deadline to respond, sent before starting court proceedings. Courts expect it, and skipping it can affect who pays the costs. Our free claim letter tool helps you draft one.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in England and Wales, and similar formal demand letters elsewhere.

/glossary/statute-of-limitations.t: Statute of limitations: Meaning and How It Works

/glossary/statute-of-limitations.lead: The US name for the law that sets the deadline for filing a lawsuit. Each state sets its own periods by type of claim, and federal claims have their own, so the same claim can have different deadlines in different states.

faq.q: What is Statute of limitations?
faq.a: The US name for the law that sets the deadline for filing a lawsuit. Each state sets its own periods by type of claim, and federal claims have their own, so the same claim can have different deadlines in different states.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in United States.

/glossary/small-claims-procedure.t: Small claims procedure: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/small-claims-procedure.d: A simpler and cheaper court procedure for low-value claims, designed so that people can bring a claim without a lawyer. The value limit and the costs…
/glossary/small-claims-procedure.lead: A simpler and cheaper court procedure for low-value claims, designed so that people can bring a claim without a lawyer. The value limit and the costs rules differ by country; in England and Wales the small claims track generally covers claims up to £10,000.

faq.q: What is Small claims procedure?
faq.a: A simpler and cheaper court procedure for low-value claims, designed so that people can bring a claim without a lawyer. The value limit and the costs rules differ by country; in England and Wales the small claims track generally covers claims up to £10,000.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: It is a general term, used in many countries.

/glossary/out-of-court-settlement.t: Out-of-court settlement: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/out-of-court-settlement.d: An agreement that ends a dispute without a court judgment, usually in exchange for a payment. Most claims settle. On a no-win-no-fee agreement, a…
/glossary/out-of-court-settlement.lead: An agreement that ends a dispute without a court judgment, usually in exchange for a payment. Most claims settle. On a no-win-no-fee agreement, a settlement normally counts as a win, so the lawyer's success fee or percentage applies to the amount agreed.

faq.q: What is Out-of-court settlement?
faq.a: An agreement that ends a dispute without a court judgment, usually in exchange for a payment. Most claims settle. On a no-win-no-fee agreement, a settlement normally counts as a win, so the lawyer's success fee or percentage applies to the amount agreed.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: It is a general term, used in many countries.

/glossary/burofax.t: Burofax: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/burofax.d: A certified communication sent through the Spanish postal service with proof of content and delivery. It is commonly used to send a formal demand before a…
/glossary/burofax.lead: A certified communication sent through the Spanish postal service with proof of content and delivery. It is commonly used to send a formal demand before a claim, and a demand received by the debtor can interrupt the limitation period.

faq.q: What is Burofax?
faq.a: A certified communication sent through the Spanish postal service with proof of content and delivery. It is commonly used to send a formal demand before a claim, and a demand received by the debtor can interrupt the limitation period.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in Spain.

/glossary/proceso-monitorio.t: Proceso monitorio: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/proceso-monitorio.d: A fast Spanish court procedure to recover a money debt backed by documents, such as invoices or a signed contract. The initial application can be filed…
/glossary/proceso-monitorio.lead: A fast Spanish court procedure to recover a money debt backed by documents, such as invoices or a signed contract. The initial application can be filed without a lawyer. If the debtor does not pay or object, the court can order enforcement.

faq.q: What is Proceso monitorio?
faq.a: A fast Spanish court procedure to recover a money debt backed by documents, such as invoices or a signed contract. The initial application can be filed without a lawyer. If the debtor does not pay or object, the court can order enforcement.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in Spain.

/glossary/european-order-for-payment.t: European order for payment: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/european-order-for-payment.d: A procedure under Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 to recover uncontested money claims across EU borders using standard forms.
/glossary/european-order-for-payment.lead: A procedure under Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 to recover uncontested money claims across EU borders using standard forms. If the debtor does not object, the order becomes enforceable in the other member states.

faq.q: What is European order for payment?
faq.a: A procedure under Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 to recover uncontested money claims across EU borders using standard forms. If the debtor does not object, the order becomes enforceable in the other member states.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in European Union (except Denmark).

/glossary/european-small-claims-procedur.t: European Small Claims Procedure: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/european-small-claims-procedur.d: A written procedure for cross-border claims of up to €5,000 under Regulation (EC) No 861/2007, using standard forms and usually without a hearing.
/glossary/european-small-claims-procedur.lead: A written procedure for cross-border claims of up to €5,000 under Regulation (EC) No 861/2007, using standard forms and usually without a hearing. A lawyer is not required.

faq.q: What is European Small Claims Procedure?
faq.a: A written procedure for cross-border claims of up to €5,000 under Regulation (EC) No 861/2007, using standard forms and usually without a hearing. A lawyer is not required.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in European Union (except Denmark).

/glossary/funding-multiple.t: Funding multiple: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/funding-multiple.d: A way of setting a litigation funder's return as a multiple of the money it invests in the case, often compared with, or combined with, a percentage of…
/glossary/funding-multiple.lead: A way of setting a litigation funder's return as a multiple of the money it invests in the case, often compared with, or combined with, a percentage of the recovery. The funding agreement should state how the return is calculated and in what order the proceeds are paid out.

faq.q: What is Funding multiple?
faq.a: A way of setting a litigation funder's return as a multiple of the money it invests in the case, often compared with, or combined with, a percentage of the recovery. The funding agreement should state how the return is calculated and in what order the proceeds are paid out.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: It is a general term, used in many countries.

/glossary/non-recourse-funding.t: Non-recourse funding: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/non-recourse-funding.d: Funding that is repaid only out of what the case recovers. If the case is lost, you owe the funder nothing. Most third-party litigation funding works this…
/glossary/non-recourse-funding.lead: Funding that is repaid only out of what the case recovers. If the case is lost, you owe the funder nothing. Most third-party litigation funding works this way, but check whether the agreement also covers the other side's costs.

faq.q: What is Non-recourse funding?
faq.a: Funding that is repaid only out of what the case recovers. If the case is lost, you owe the funder nothing. Most third-party litigation funding works this way, but check whether the agreement also covers the other side's costs.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: It is a general term, used in many countries.

/glossary/security-for-costs.t: Security for costs: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/security-for-costs.d: An order requiring a claimant to pay money into court or give a guarantee to cover the defendant's costs if the claim fails, for example when the claimant…
/glossary/security-for-costs.lead: An order requiring a claimant to pay money into court or give a guarantee to cover the defendant's costs if the claim fails, for example when the claimant lives abroad or is a company that may not be able to pay. Funders and ATE insurers can sometimes provide it.

faq.q: What is Security for costs?
faq.a: An order requiring a claimant to pay money into court or give a guarantee to cover the defendant's costs if the claim fails, for example when the claimant lives abroad or is a company that may not be able to pay. Funders and ATE insurers can sometimes provide it.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in England and Wales, Ireland, Australia and other common-law systems.

/glossary/pactum-de-quota-litis.t: Pactum de Quota Litis: Meaning and Where It Is Allowed
/glossary/pactum-de-quota-litis.d: Latin for an agreement under which a lawyer's fee is only a share of what the client wins. Many civil-law countries forbid it while allowing a success…
/glossary/pactum-de-quota-litis.lead: Latin for an agreement under which a lawyer's fee is only a share of what the client wins. Many civil-law countries forbid it while allowing a success bonus on top of a base fee; Spain has allowed it since 2008.

faq.q: What is Pactum de quota litis?
faq.a: Latin for an agreement under which a lawyer's fee is only a share of what the client wins. Many civil-law countries forbid it while allowing a success bonus on top of a base fee; Spain has allowed it since 2008.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in Civil-law countries.

/glossary/honorarios-de-exito.t: Honorários de êxito: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/honorarios-de-exito.d: A success fee agreed between client and lawyer, often alongside a smaller fixed fee. It is separate from the honorários de sucumbência, the costs a court…
/glossary/honorarios-de-exito.lead: A success fee agreed between client and lawyer, often alongside a smaller fixed fee. It is separate from the honorários de sucumbência, the costs a court orders the losing side to pay to the winner's lawyer.

faq.q: What is Honorários de êxito?
faq.a: A success fee agreed between client and lawyer, often alongside a smaller fixed fee. It is separate from the honorários de sucumbência, the costs a court orders the losing side to pay to the winner's lawyer.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in Brazil.

/glossary/prozessfinanzierung.t: Prozessfinanzierung: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/prozessfinanzierung.d: The German term for third-party litigation funding: a funder pays the court and lawyer costs, and the other side's costs if the case is lost, in return…
/glossary/prozessfinanzierung.lead: The German term for third-party litigation funding: a funder pays the court and lawyer costs, and the other side's costs if the case is lost, in return for a share of the proceeds agreed in the contract. Funders usually look for larger claims with good prospects.

faq.q: What is Prozessfinanzierung?
faq.a: The German term for third-party litigation funding: a funder pays the court and lawyer costs, and the other side's costs if the case is lost, in return for a share of the proceeds agreed in the contract. Funders usually look for larger claims with good prospects.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.

/glossary/no-foil-no-fee.t: No foil, no fee: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/no-foil-no-fee.d: The Irish form of no-win-no-fee: the solicitor charges no fee if the case is lost. Irish solicitors may not charge a percentage of the damages, and you…
/glossary/no-foil-no-fee.lead: The Irish form of no-win-no-fee: the solicitor charges no fee if the case is lost. Irish solicitors may not charge a percentage of the damages, and you may still face the other side's costs if you lose.

faq.q: What is No foil, no fee?
faq.a: The Irish form of no-win-no-fee: the solicitor charges no fee if the case is lost. Irish solicitors may not charge a percentage of the damages, and you may still face the other side's costs if you lose.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in Ireland.

/glossary/claims-management-company.t: Claims management company (CMC): Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/claims-management-company.d: A business that handles claims for a share of the compensation, often passing them to a law firm. In Great Britain, CMCs have been regulated by the…
/glossary/claims-management-company.lead: A business that handles claims for a share of the compensation, often passing them to a law firm. In Great Britain, CMCs have been regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority since 2019. Many claims can be made directly for free, so check before signing.

faq.q: What is Claims management company?
faq.a: A business that handles claims for a share of the compensation, often passing them to a law firm. In Great Britain, CMCs have been regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority since 2019. Many claims can be made directly for free, so check before signing.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in United Kingdom.

/glossary/costs-follow-the-event.t: Costs follow the event: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/costs-follow-the-event.d: The general principle that the losing party pays the winning party's legal costs, usually only part of them, as assessed by the court.
/glossary/costs-follow-the-event.lead: The general principle that the losing party pays the winning party's legal costs, usually only part of them, as assessed by the court. Courts can depart from it, for example when the winner behaved unreasonably.

faq.q: What is Costs follow the event?
faq.a: The general principle that the losing party pays the winning party's legal costs, usually only part of them, as assessed by the court. Courts can depart from it, for example when the winner behaved unreasonably.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in England and Wales, Ireland and many other countries.

/glossary/american-rule-on-costs.t: American rule on costs: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/american-rule-on-costs.d: The principle that each side pays its own lawyer whatever the result, unless a statute or contract says otherwise. It is one reason contingency fees work…
/glossary/american-rule-on-costs.lead: The principle that each side pays its own lawyer whatever the result, unless a statute or contract says otherwise. It is one reason contingency fees work well in the US: losing usually does not mean paying the other side's lawyer.

faq.q: What is American rule on costs?
faq.a: The principle that each side pays its own lawyer whatever the result, unless a statute or contract says otherwise. It is one reason contingency fees work well in the US: losing usually does not mean paying the other side's lawyer.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in United States.

/glossary/disclosure-of-documents.t: Disclosure of documents: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/disclosure-of-documents.d: The stage of a case in which each side must reveal relevant documents, including some that harm its own case. It can be costly and time-consuming, which…
/glossary/disclosure-of-documents.lead: The stage of a case in which each side must reveal relevant documents, including some that harm its own case. It can be costly and time-consuming, which is one reason lawyers and funders weigh it when deciding whether to take a case.

faq.q: What is Disclosure of documents?
faq.a: The stage of a case in which each side must reveal relevant documents, including some that harm its own case. It can be costly and time-consuming, which is one reason lawyers and funders weigh it when deciding whether to take a case.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in England and Wales; called discovery in the United States.

/glossary/late-payment-interest.t: Late payment interest: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/late-payment-interest.d: Statutory interest a business can charge on late payment by another business. Under the EU Late Payment Directive the rate is at least 8 percentage points…
/glossary/late-payment-interest.lead: Statutory interest a business can charge on late payment by another business. Under the EU Late Payment Directive the rate is at least 8 percentage points above the reference rate, plus a fixed €40 compensation per invoice; the UK has its own similar rules. Our free calculator works it out.

faq.q: What is Late payment interest?
faq.a: Statutory interest a business can charge on late payment by another business. Under the EU Late Payment Directive the rate is at least 8 percentage points above the reference rate, plus a fixed €40 compensation per invoice; the UK has its own similar rules. Our free calculator works it out.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in European Union and United Kingdom.

/glossary/eu261-flight-compensation.t: EU261 flight compensation: Meaning and How It Works
/glossary/eu261-flight-compensation.d: Fixed compensation under Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 of €250, €400 or €600 depending on flight distance, for long delays at arrival, late cancellations…
/glossary/eu261-flight-compensation.lead: Fixed compensation under Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 of €250, €400 or €600 depending on flight distance, for long delays at arrival, late cancellations and denied boarding, unless the airline proves extraordinary circumstances. The UK version pays similar amounts in pounds.

faq.q: What is EU261 flight compensation?
faq.a: Fixed compensation under Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 of €250, €400 or €600 depending on flight distance, for long delays at arrival, late cancellations and denied boarding, unless the airline proves extraordinary circumstances. The UK version pays similar amounts in pounds.

faq.q: Where is the term used?
faq.a: Mainly in European Union, and flights covered by the UK version.

faq.q: How do I get no-win-no-fee clients through JuriMatch?
faq.a: Create an account with your work email, claim your firm's listing (or create one) and set the case types, countries and minimum claim value you accept. When a claimant's case fits those settings, you receive an anonymised, pre-scored brief in the lawyer portal. If you accept, the claimant's contact details unlock and you agree terms directly with them.

faq.q: How do I claim my firm's listing?
faq.a: Search for your firm on the join page and claim it. Claims are approved instantly when your email domain matches the firm's website; otherwise our team reviews the request. If your firm is not listed, you can create a new profile instead.

faq.q: How does verification work?
faq.a: We check that your website and contact details match the listing, that you offer no-win-no-fee, contingency, conditional-fee or funded work for the case types you list, and, where you provide one, your regulator registration. Verified firms are re-checked at least once a year. Verification status cannot be bought.

faq.q: What does it cost?
faq.a: Nothing for founding firms: no listing fee, no referral fee and no share of your fees. Claimants pay JuriMatch for matching; you agree your own fees with the client. Any fee a firm pays JuriMatch would be set out in writing before it applies.

faq.q: Is this compatible with professional rules on referral fees?
faq.a: JuriMatch does not take referral fees or share fees with firms, so it works like a directory and case-routing service. No money passes between JuriMatch and your firm for an introduction, and the claimant chooses which firm to instruct. JuriMatch will not accept any payment that the professional rules applying to you prohibit. You remain responsible for checking your own rules.

faq.q: Who is responsible for advice, conflict checks and the fee agreement?
faq.a: You are. JuriMatch is not a law firm and does not give legal advice. Whether to accept a case, conflict checks, client identification, engagement letters and fee agreements are your responsibility, and the lawyer-client or funding relationship is formed directly between you and the claimant.

faq.q: What do I see before accepting a case?
faq.a: An anonymised brief: claim type, estimated value, jurisdictions, evidence flags and a 0 to 100 case score. The counterparty's type and country are shown, but not its name. You can ask questions through JuriMatch before accepting. The claimant's contact details unlock only when you accept.

faq.q: How does matching work?
faq.a: A case is routed to you when it fits your preferences: the claimant's or the defendant's country is one of your jurisdictions, the claim type is one you accept, and the amount is at or above your minimum. Leaving a filter empty accepts everything in that dimension. A case can be sent to a small number of matching firms so the claimant has a real choice; each firm sees the same anonymised brief and the claimant decides who to work with.

faq.q: How is the case score worked out?
faq.a: Claimants complete a structured questionnaire and can upload documents. We score each case from 0 to 100 across documentation, jurisdiction, recoverability, economics and complexity, and add an evidence checklist and deadline flags. The score is a triage aid, not legal advice: you make your own assessment.

faq.q: Can I decline a case?
faq.a: Yes, any case, at any time before you accept it. A reason is optional and there are no quotas or penalties.

faq.q: How do I pause new cases?
faq.a: In the lawyer portal, open Preferences and turn off "Accepting new cases". Routing stops until you turn it back on, and cases you already have stay in your inbox. You can also change your case types, countries and minimum claim value there at any time.

faq.q: Can I remove my listing?
faq.a: Yes. You can stop using JuriMatch and ask us to remove your listing at any time through the firm listing request page or by email to our legal team.

faq.q: How is claimant data protected?
faq.a: Briefs are anonymised and contact details are released only to a firm that accepts. You must not try to identify a claimant from a brief, and you may use claimant information only to assess and act on that claimant's matter: no marketing, resale, profiling or sharing. For data you receive you act as an independent controller and must follow applicable data-protection law, including GDPR where it applies, and your confidentiality duties.

/fees/cfa-vs-dba.t: CFA vs DBA: Which No-Win-No-Fee Agreement Is Better?
/fees/cfa-vs-dba.d: Conditional fee agreements and damages-based agreements compared: how each is paid, the legal caps, what you pay if you win or lose, and which suits your…
/fees/cfa-vs-dba.h1: Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs Damages-based agreement (DBA)
/fees/cfa-vs-dba.lead: Both mean you pay your own solicitor nothing if you lose. Under a CFA you pay normal fees plus a capped success fee if you win; under a DBA the solicitor takes a capped percentage of your damages instead. Neither covers the other side's costs, which is what ATE insurance is for.
crumbs: Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs Damages-based agreement (DBA)
facts: What the lawyer gets if you win
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Normal (base) fees plus a success fee. Damages-based agreement (DBA): An agreed percentage of the damages.
Legal cap

Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Success fee up to 100% of base costs; in personal injury, up to 25% of certain damages. Damages-based agreement (DBA): Including VAT: 25% in personal injury, 35% in employment, 50% in other claims.
Costs paid by the other side

Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Usually cover much of the base fees; the success fee normally comes out of your damages. Damages-based agreement (DBA): Count towards the agreed percentage, so you usually pay the difference from your damages.
If you lose

Conditional fee agreement (CFA): No fee to your solicitor; the other side's costs unless protected or insured. Damages-based agreement (DBA): No fee to your solicitor; the other side's costs unless protected or insured.
Common in
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Personal injury, professional negligence, commercial claims. Damages-based agreement (DBA): Employment claims and some commercial claims.

faq.q: Is a CFA or a DBA cheaper?
faq.a: It depends on the size of the damages and how much of the costs you recover. With high damages and low costs a CFA is often cheaper; with low recoverable costs a DBA can work out better. Ask the solicitor to model both on your figures.

faq.q: Do I pay anything if I lose under a CFA or DBA?
faq.a: Not to your own solicitor, if the agreement says so. You may still owe disbursements such as court fees and experts, and the other side's costs unless you are protected (for example by QOCS in most personal injury claims) or insured with ATE insurance.

faq.q: Can a solicitor change from a CFA to a DBA mid-case?
faq.a: Only by a new written agreement that you sign. Read how any work already done is treated before agreeing.

/fees/contingency-fee-vs-litigation-fund.t: Contingency Fee vs Litigation Funding: Which Is Right for Your Claim?
/fees/contingency-fee-vs-litigation-fund.d: Contingency fees and third-party litigation funding compared: who pays the costs, what each takes from a win, typical claim sizes, and what happens if you lose.
/fees/contingency-fee-vs-litigation-fund.lead: With a contingency fee your own lawyer works without being paid unless you recover. With litigation funding a separate company pays the legal costs, and often the risk of the other side's costs, in return for a share of the recovery. Funders usually look for larger claims.
facts: Who carries the cost of the case
Contingency fee: Your lawyer, by working unpaid until the end. Litigation funding: A third-party funder, who pays the lawyers as the case goes.
What they take if you win
Contingency fee: An agreed percentage of the recovery. Litigation funding: A multiple of the money invested or a percentage of the recovery, whichever the contract says.
If you lose
Contingency fee: No lawyer fee; expenses and the other side's costs may still apply. Litigation funding: Nothing to the funder (non-recourse); many funders also cover the other side's costs.
Typical claim size
Contingency fee: From small to large claims. Litigation funding: Usually larger claims; funders often want damages of around ten times the expected costs.
Where it is allowed
Contingency fee: Widely in the US, Canada and others; restricted in many European countries. Litigation funding: Most major jurisdictions, with rules that differ by country.

faq.q: Can I use a contingency fee and litigation funding together?
faq.a: Sometimes. A funder may pay part of the costs while the law firm takes a reduced fee plus a success element. The total taken from your recovery should be set out in writing before you sign.

faq.q: Do I have to repay a litigation funder if I lose?
faq.a: Normally not: most funding is non-recourse, so the funder loses its investment. Check the agreement for exceptions such as misconduct or abandoning the case.

faq.q: Which leaves me more money if I win?
faq.a: It depends on the percentages, the length of the case and the multiple the funder charges. Ask for a worked example at several outcomes and timelines.

/fees/no-win-no-fee-vs-hourly-fees.lead: Under no win, no fee you pay your own lawyer nothing if you lose, but give up a share of a win. Paying by the hour costs money whatever the outcome, but you keep the whole award. No win, no fee suits claimants who cannot or do not want to fund the risk.
crumbs: No win, no fee vs Hourly fees
facts: If you lose
No win, no fee: No fee to your own lawyer (expenses and the other side's costs may apply). Hourly fees: All your lawyer's fees, plus possibly the other side's costs.
If you win
No win, no fee: A share of the recovery or a success fee. Hourly fees: The fees already paid; you keep the whole award.
Cash needed during the case
No win, no fee: Little or none. Hourly fees: Regular invoices, often from the start.
Who carries the risk
No win, no fee: Mostly the lawyer. Hourly fees: You.
Case selection
No win, no fee: The lawyer only takes cases with good prospects. Hourly fees: The lawyer can act on cases with lower prospects.

faq.q: Is no win no fee really free if I lose?
faq.a: You pay your own lawyer nothing if the agreement says so, but you may still owe expenses such as court fees and experts, and in most countries outside the US the other side's costs. Ask who covers these before signing.

faq.q: Why would a lawyer turn down my case on no win no fee?
faq.a: Because they are taking the risk. Lawyers look at the chances of winning, the amount at stake, whether the other side can pay, and the time it will take.

faq.q: Can I switch from hourly fees to no win no fee?
faq.a: Sometimes, with a new written agreement. A new firm may also take over a case on success terms after reviewing it.

/fees/cfa-vs-ate-insurance.t: CFA vs ATE Insurance: What Each One Covers If You Lose
/fees/cfa-vs-ate-insurance.d: A CFA and ATE insurance protect against different costs. What each covers if you win or lose, who pays the premium and why many claims in England and…
/fees/cfa-vs-ate-insurance.h1: Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs After-the-event (ATE) insurance
/fees/cfa-vs-ate-insurance.lead: They cover different risks and are often used together. A CFA means you pay your own solicitor no fee if you lose. ATE insurance pays the other side's costs, and often your own expenses, if you lose. A CFA alone leaves you exposed to the other side's costs.
crumbs: Conditional fee agreement (CFA) vs After-the-event (ATE) insurance
facts: What it protects you from
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Your own solicitor's fees if you lose. After-the-event (ATE) insurance: The other side's costs, and often your own expenses, if you lose.
Who provides it
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Your solicitor. After-the-event (ATE) insurance: An insurer, usually arranged by your solicitor.
What it costs if you win

Conditional fee agreement (CFA): A success fee on top of the base fees, capped by law. After-the-event (ATE) insurance: A premium, normally paid out of your damages; it is usually not recoverable from the other side.
What it costs if you lose
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): No fee to your solicitor if the agreement says so. After-the-event (ATE) insurance: Often nothing: many premiums are deferred and payable only if you win.
Needed in personal injury claims
Conditional fee agreement (CFA): Common. After-the-event (ATE) insurance: Less often, because QOCS usually protects claimants from the other side's costs.

faq.q: Do I need ATE insurance if I have a CFA?
faq.a: Often yes, outside personal injury. A CFA only deals with your own solicitor's fees. If you lose, a court can still order you to pay the other side's costs, and ATE insurance is the usual protection.

faq.q: Who pays the ATE premium?
faq.a: Usually you, out of your damages if you win. Many policies defer the premium and make it payable only if the claim succeeds, so nothing is due if you lose. Check the policy.

faq.q: Can my solicitor arrange ATE insurance?
faq.a: Yes, solicitors usually arrange it with an insurer they work with. Ask what it covers, the limit of cover, the premium and when it is payable.

/fees/contingency-fee-vs-fixed-fee.t: Contingency Fee vs Fixed Fee: Which Costs You Less?
/fees/contingency-fee-vs-fixed-fee.d: A contingency fee (cuota litis) against a fixed fee for a legal claim: what you pay if you win or lose, cash needed upfront, and which suits small, large…
/fees/contingency-fee-vs-fixed-fee.lead: A fixed fee is a set price agreed in advance and payable whatever the result. A contingency fee is a share of what you recover and nothing if you lose. Fixed fees suit simple, predictable work; contingency fees suit claims where you want the lawyer to share the risk.
facts: If you lose
Contingency fee: No fee to your lawyer (expenses and the other side's costs may apply). Fixed fee: The full fixed fee.
If you win
Contingency fee: An agreed share of the recovery. Fixed fee: The fixed fee only; you keep the rest of the award.
Cash needed upfront
Contingency fee: Little or none. Fixed fee: Often part or all of the fee at the start.
Predictability
Contingency fee: You know the percentage, not the final amount. Fixed fee: You know the price, unless the work goes beyond what was agreed.
Typical use
Contingency fee: Money claims with good prospects: injury, fraud, consumer and commercial claims. Fixed fee: Defined tasks: a demand letter, a simple debt claim, a contract review.

faq.q: Can I combine a fixed fee and a success fee?
faq.a: Often, yes. Many lawyers in Spain, France, Italy and Brazil charge a smaller fixed fee plus a success fee. In some countries this mix is the only form allowed.

faq.q: What does a fixed fee usually not include?
faq.a: Court fees, expert reports and the other side's costs if you lose. Ask exactly which steps the fixed fee covers and what happens if the case goes further, such as to an appeal.

faq.q: Is a contingency fee always more expensive if I win?
faq.a: Not always. It depends on the size of the award and how much work the case needs. Ask the lawyer to show you both options on your figures.

/claims/ryanair.t: Claims against Ryanair: delays, cancellations and refunds
/claims/ryanair.d: How to claim against Ryanair for delayed or cancelled flights under EU261 and UK261, refunds and baggage: steps, evidence, deadlines and when a lawyer helps.
/claims/ryanair.h1: Claims against Ryanair: delays, cancellations and refunds
/claims/ryanair.lead: Ryanair is an Irish airline, so its flights from or to the EU are generally covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, and flights from the UK by UK261. Most passenger claims against it are about long delays, cancellations, refunds and baggage. This guide explains how those claims usually work.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer to claim compensation from Ryanair?
faq.a: Usually not for the first step: you can claim directly with the airline for free. A claim company or no-win-no-fee lawyer can help if the airline refuses or does not reply, in exchange for a share of the compensation.

faq.q: Does Ryanair have to pay if the delay was caused by weather or strikes?
faq.a: Not if the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided with reasonable measures, such as severe weather. Courts have held that strikes by the airline's own staff are not normally extraordinary, while strikes by third parties such as air traffic controllers can be. Each case depends on its facts.

faq.q: How much compensation can I get?
faq.a: Under EU261 the fixed amounts are 250, 400 or 600 euros depending on distance (UK261 uses pounds). Our flight compensation calculator shows which band applies. Refunds and expenses for care are separate from compensation.

facts: Delay and cancellation compensation

Under EU Regulation 261/2004 (and its UK copy, UK261), passengers can claim fixed compensation for long delays at arrival, late cancellations and denied boarding, unless the airline shows the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances such as severe weather or air traffic control restrictions. The amount depends on the flight distance.
Refunds and care

When a flight is cancelled, passengers are entitled to choose between a refund and re-routing, and to care (meals, and a hotel if an overnight stay is needed) while they wait. Customers have brought complaints where refunds were slow or only vouchers were offered.
Baggage
Lost, delayed or damaged luggage is covered by the Montreal Convention, which has short notice periods: report it at the airport and send a written claim to the airline quickly.
Extra charges
Some passengers have brought complaints about fees for bags, seats or check-in. These are usually treated as consumer complaints rather than EU261 claims.
Deadlines

There is no single EU deadline for flight compensation: the limitation period is set by the law of the country where you bring the claim, and it varies considerably between countries. Baggage claims under the Montreal Convention have much shorter notice periods (days, not years) and a two-year limit for court action. Use the limitation checker for an indicative deadline in your country, and act early: evidence such as boarding passes and emails is easier to gather now. Indicative period in Ireland (contract claims): 6 years.

/claims/lufthansa.lead: Lufthansa is a German airline, so its flights are generally covered by EU Regulation 261/2004, including long-haul flights departing from the EU. Passenger claims are mostly about long delays, cancellations, missed connections, refunds and baggage. In Germany, independent conciliation bodies handle passenger disputes free of charge for passengers.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer to claim compensation from Lufthansa?
faq.a: Usually not for the first step: you can claim directly with the airline for free. A claim company or no-win-no-fee lawyer can help if the airline refuses or does not reply, in exchange for a share of the compensation.

faq.q: Does Lufthansa have to pay if the delay was caused by weather or strikes?
faq.a: Not if the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided with reasonable measures, such as severe weather. Courts have held that strikes by the airline's own staff are not normally extraordinary, while strikes by third parties such as air traffic controllers can be. Each case depends on its facts.

faq.q: How much compensation can I get?
faq.a: Under EU261 the fixed amounts are 250, 400 or 600 euros depending on distance (UK261 uses pounds). Our flight compensation calculator shows which band applies. Refunds and expenses for care are separate from compensation.

facts: Delay and cancellation compensation

Under EU Regulation 261/2004 (and its UK copy, UK261), passengers can claim fixed compensation for long delays at arrival, late cancellations and denied boarding, unless the airline shows the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances such as severe weather or air traffic control restrictions. The amount depends on the flight distance.
Missed connections
When connecting flights are booked together and you reach the final destination more than three hours late, compensation is generally calculated on the distance to the final destination.
Refunds and care

When a flight is cancelled, passengers are entitled to choose between a refund and re-routing, and to care (meals, and a hotel if an overnight stay is needed) while they wait. Customers have brought complaints where refunds were slow or only vouchers were offered.
Baggage
Lost, delayed or damaged luggage is covered by the Montreal Convention, which has short notice periods: report it at the airport and send a written claim to the airline quickly.
Deadlines

There is no single EU deadline for flight compensation: the limitation period is set by the law of the country where you bring the claim, and it varies considerably between countries. Baggage claims under the Montreal Convention have much shorter notice periods (days, not years) and a two-year limit for court action. In Germany, the regular limitation period is three years from the end of the year in which the claim arose. Use the limitation checker for other countries. Indicative period in Germany (contract claims): 3 years (from knowledge).

/claims/santander.t: Claims against Santander: mortgages, cards and Banco Popular
/claims/santander.d: What customers claim against Santander in Spain (floor clauses, mortgage costs, revolving cards, Banco Popular), how to complain and when a lawyer helps.
/claims/santander.h1: Claims against Santander: mortgages, cards and Banco Popular
/claims/santander.lead: Banco Santander is one of Spain's largest banks and acquired Banco Popular in 2017. Like other Spanish banks, it has faced consumer claims over mortgage terms and credit products, and former Banco Popular investors brought claims after Popular's 2017 resolution. This guide explains the usual claims and routes in Spain.

faq.q: Do I have to complain to Santander before going to court?
faq.a: In practice, yes. A written complaint to the bank's customer service is required before you can go to the Banco de España complaints service, and since April 2025 most civil claims in Spain require a prior attempt to settle. A documented written complaint usually serves both purposes.

faq.q: Do lawyers take these cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
faq.a: Many do, especially floor clause and mortgage expense claims, because when the bank loses in full it is normally ordered to pay costs. Ask for the fee agreement (hoja de encargo) in writing, including what happens if the bank settles early.

faq.q: Can I still claim if I have paid off the loan?
faq.a: Often yes. Having repaid or cancelled a mortgage does not by itself prevent a claim about an unfair term, but any later agreement or waiver you signed needs to be reviewed.

facts: Floor clauses (cláusulas suelo)

Mortgage terms that set a minimum interest rate. Since 2013 Spanish courts have held them void where they were not transparent, and since the CJEU's December 2016 ruling banks must repay everything charged under a void clause, with interest.
Mortgage set-up costs (gastos de hipoteca)
Customers have claimed back part of the notary, registry, agency and valuation costs charged when the mortgage was signed, after courts held clauses passing all costs to the customer to be unfair.
Revolving credit cards
Claims that the interest rate was usurious or that the cost of the card was not explained clearly. The Supreme Court has ruled on how to compare revolving rates with the market average.
IRPH-indexed mortgages
Claims about mortgages indexed to IRPH instead of Euribor, where the question is whether the bank explained the index and its effect transparently.
Banco Popular shares and bonds

Banco Popular was resolved by the European authorities in June 2017 and sold to Santander. Shareholders and bondholders who lost their investment have brought claims, mainly arguing that they were misinformed when they bought. Outcomes have depended on when and how the investment was made.
Deadlines

In Spain, the Supreme Court and the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) have held that the action to declare an unfair term void in a consumer contract does not expire. The time limit to recover money already paid is more debated: the CJEU has said it cannot start running before the consumer could know the term was unfair. Deadlines differ by product and are still developing through case law, so do not wait: get documents together and take advice early. Indicative period in Spain (contract claims): 5 years.

/claims/volkswagen.t: VW Emissions Claims: Dieselgate Compensation Explained
/claims/volkswagen.d: How owners have claimed against Volkswagen over diesel emissions (dieselgate): who could claim, group actions, deadlines and how no-win-no-fee lawyers work.
/claims/volkswagen.h1: Claims against Volkswagen: the diesel emissions scandal
/claims/volkswagen.lead: In September 2015 Volkswagen admitted that software in some of its diesel engines, mainly the EA189 engine used across the VW, Audi, SEAT and Skoda brands, made the cars perform differently in emissions tests than on the road. Owners in many countries have since brought individual and group claims. This guide explains how those claims have generally worked.

faq.q: Can I still claim against Volkswagen for dieselgate?
faq.a: It depends on the country, the engine, when you bought the car and whether you joined a group action. In some countries ordinary deadlines for EA189 cars have passed; in others, or for other engines, claims may still be possible. Get a deadline check before anything else.

faq.q: Do I need to still own the car?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Courts in some countries have allowed claims by buyers who have since sold the car, with the sale price taken into account.

faq.q: Do lawyers take diesel claims on a no-win-no-fee basis?
faq.a: Many do, often with litigation funding or legal expenses insurance, because claims are numerous and similar. Read how the fee is calculated and what happens if you withdraw.

facts: Damages for buyers

Owners have claimed the car was worth less than they paid, or that they would not have bought it had they known. In Germany, the Federal Court of Justice (BGH) ruled in May 2020 that buyers of cars with the EA189 engine could claim damages against Volkswagen, with a deduction for the use they had of the car.
Group and collective actions

Consumer associations and claimant groups have run collective cases in several countries, including a model declaratory action in Germany that ended in a settlement in 2020, and group litigation in England and Wales that settled in 2022 without an admission of liability.
Other engines and brands
Claims have also been brought about other diesel engines and brands in the group. Whether a particular car is affected depends on the engine and model year.
Deadlines

Limitation periods depend on the country, and the start date often depends on when buyers knew or should have known about the issue. Many claims about vehicles affected in 2015 have reached or passed the ordinary limit in some countries. Group actions have their own registration or opt-in deadlines. Use the limitation checker and ask a lawyer before assuming your claim is still open. Indicative period in Germany (non-contractual damages (tort)): 3 years (from knowledge).

/claims/mercedes-benz.t: Mercedes Diesel Claims: Emissions, Recalls and Group Claims
/claims/mercedes-benz.d: How owners have claimed against Mercedes-Benz over diesel emissions: recalls, the 2023 CJEU ruling, group claims, deadlines and no-win-no-fee options.
/claims/mercedes-benz.lead: Owners of some Mercedes-Benz diesel cars have brought claims arguing that emissions controls worked differently on the road than in tests, for example through temperature-dependent settings. German authorities ordered recalls of some models, and the manufacturer has disputed that its vehicles contained unlawful defeat devices. This guide explains how these claims have generally worked.

faq.q: Is my Mercedes affected?
faq.a: It depends on the engine, model and emissions class. Recall letters and official vehicle checkers are a starting point; a lawyer or claims group can check your specific car.

faq.q: How much could I get?
faq.a: There is no fixed amount. In Germany, courts following the 2023 CJEU ruling have generally awarded a percentage of the purchase price for negligence claims; elsewhere it depends on national law and the claim.

faq.q: Do lawyers take these cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
faq.a: Many do, often backed by litigation funding or legal expenses insurance. Ask how the fee is calculated and what happens if the claim fails.

facts: Damages for buyers in the EU

In March 2023 the Court of Justice of the EU ruled (case C-100/21, against Mercedes-Benz Group) that buyers can claim damages from a manufacturer that negligently installed an unlawful defeat device. Following that ruling, the German Federal Court of Justice (BGH) allowed damages for negligence, generally between 5% and 15% of the purchase price, depending on the case.
Group claims in England and Wales
Group claims over diesel emissions involving several manufacturers, Mercedes-Benz among them, have been brought in the High Court in London.
Which cars are affected
Claims depend on the specific engine, model and emissions class. A recall or software update letter is a useful starting point, but not every recalled car gives rise to a claim, and vice versa.
Deadlines

Limitation periods depend on the country, and the start date often depends on when buyers knew or should have known about the issue. Many claims about vehicles affected in 2015 have reached or passed the ordinary limit in some countries. Group actions have their own registration or opt-in deadlines. Use the limitation checker and ask a lawyer before assuming your claim is still open. Indicative period in Germany (non-contractual damages (tort)): 3 years (from knowledge).

/claims/jet2.lead: Jet2.com is a UK leisure airline based in Leeds, often sold with Jet2holidays packages. Its flights from the UK are covered by UK261 and its flights from EU airports back to the UK by EU261. Package holidaymakers also have rights against the tour operator.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer to claim compensation from Jet2?
faq.a: Usually not for the first step: you can claim directly with the airline for free. A claim company or no-win-no-fee lawyer can help if the airline refuses or does not reply, in exchange for a share of the compensation.

faq.q: Does Jet2 have to pay if the delay was caused by weather or strikes?
faq.a: Not if the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided with reasonable measures, such as severe weather. Courts have held that strikes by the airline's own staff are not normally extraordinary, while strikes by third parties such as air traffic controllers can be. Each case depends on its facts.

faq.q: How much compensation can I get?
faq.a: Under EU261 the fixed amounts are 250, 400 or 600 euros depending on distance (UK261 uses pounds). Our flight compensation calculator shows which band applies. Refunds and expenses for care are separate from compensation.

facts: Delay and cancellation compensation

Under EU Regulation 261/2004 (and its UK copy, UK261), passengers can claim fixed compensation for long delays at arrival, late cancellations and denied boarding, unless the airline shows the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances such as severe weather or air traffic control restrictions. The amount depends on the flight distance.
Refunds and care

When a flight is cancelled, passengers are entitled to choose between a refund and re-routing, and to care (meals, and a hotel if an overnight stay is needed) while they wait. Customers have brought complaints where refunds were slow or only vouchers were offered.
Baggage
Lost, delayed or damaged luggage is covered by the Montreal Convention, which has short notice periods: report it at the airport and send a written claim to the airline quickly.
Deadlines

There is no single EU deadline for flight compensation: the limitation period is set by the law of the country where you bring the claim, and it varies considerably between countries. Baggage claims under the Montreal Convention have much shorter notice periods (days, not years) and a two-year limit for court action. Use the limitation checker for an indicative deadline in your country, and act early: evidence such as boarding passes and emails is easier to gather now. Indicative period in the United Kingdom (contract claims): 6 years.

/claims/bankinter.t: Claims against Bankinter: floor clauses, mortgage costs and cards
/claims/bankinter.d: What customers claim against Bankinter in Spain (floor clauses, mortgage costs, IRPH, cards), the free complaint route and deadlines.
/claims/bankinter.h1: Claims against Bankinter: floor clauses, mortgage costs and cards
/claims/bankinter.lead: Bankinter is a Spanish bank known for its mortgage and private banking business. Besides the mortgage terms common to Spanish banks, customers have brought claims over multi-currency mortgages (hipotecas multidivisa) linked to foreign currencies such as the Swiss franc or the yen. This guide explains the usual claims and routes in Spain.

faq.q: Do I have to complain to Bankinter before going to court?
faq.a: In practice, yes. A written complaint to the bank's customer service is required before you can go to the Banco de España complaints service, and since April 2025 most civil claims in Spain require a prior attempt to settle. A documented written complaint usually serves both purposes.

faq.q: Do lawyers take these cases on a no-win-no-fee basis?
faq.a: Many do, especially floor clause and mortgage expense claims, because when the bank loses in full it is normally ordered to pay costs. Ask for the fee agreement (hoja de encargo) in writing, including what happens if the bank settles early.

faq.q: Can I still claim if I have paid off the loan?
faq.a: Often yes. Having repaid or cancelled a mortgage does not by itself prevent a claim about an unfair term, but any later agreement or waiver you signed needs to be reviewed.

facts: Floor clauses (cláusulas suelo)

Mortgage terms that set a minimum interest rate. Since 2013 Spanish courts have held them void where they were not transparent, and since the CJEU's December 2016 ruling banks must repay everything charged under a void clause, with interest.
Mortgage set-up costs (gastos de hipoteca)
Customers have claimed back part of the notary, registry, agency and valuation costs charged when the mortgage was signed, after courts held clauses passing all costs to the customer to be unfair.
Revolving credit cards
Claims that the interest rate was usurious or that the cost of the card was not explained clearly. The Supreme Court has ruled on how to compare revolving rates with the market average.
IRPH-indexed mortgages
Claims about mortgages indexed to IRPH instead of Euribor, where the question is whether the bank explained the index and its effect transparently.
Multi-currency mortgages

Mortgages repaid in or indexed to a foreign currency. Customers have claimed that the currency risk was not explained clearly; Spanish courts have annulled the currency clause where the bank could not show it gave enough information.
Deadlines

In Spain, the Supreme Court and the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) have held that the action to declare an unfair term void in a consumer contract does not expire. The time limit to recover money already paid is more debated: the CJEU has said it cannot start running before the consumer could know the term was unfair. Deadlines differ by product and are still developing through case law, so do not wait: get documents together and take advice early. Indicative period in Spain (contract claims): 5 years.

/claims/pko-bp.h1: Claims against PKO Bank Polski: Swiss franc mortgages
/claims/pko-bp.lead: PKO Bank Polski is Poland's largest bank. It is one of the banks that hold Swiss franc mortgage portfolios, and many borrowers have brought claims about the exchange-rate clauses in those loans. This guide explains how those claims generally work.

faq.q: Can I still sue PKO Bank Polski if I have repaid the Swiss franc loan?
faq.a: Often yes. Borrowers who have repaid their loan have brought claims to recover what they overpaid, but the deadline question needs checking for your dates.

faq.q: Do lawyers take these cases on a success fee?
faq.a: Many Polish firms offer a fixed fee plus a success fee, or a success fee only. Ask for the agreement in writing and how the fee is calculated if the bank settles.

faq.q: What did the CJEU decide about bank remuneration?
faq.a: In June 2023 (case C-520/21) the Court held that, when a loan contract is annulled because of unfair terms, EU law precludes the bank from claiming compensation beyond the return of the capital and interest on it from when the payment was demanded.

facts: Swiss franc mortgages (kredyty frankowe)

Borrowers with mortgages indexed to or denominated in Swiss francs have claimed that the exchange-rate clauses were unfair because the bank set the rate and did not explain the currency risk. In Dziubak (C-260/18, October 2019) the Court of Justice of the EU held that a court may annul the whole contract where it cannot continue without the unfair term.
What happens if the contract is annulled

Both sides return what they received: the borrower the capital, the bank the instalments. In June 2023 (C-520/21) the CJEU held that EU law precludes the bank from claiming remuneration beyond the capital it lent, and Polish courts have since applied that ruling.
Settlements offered by banks
Several banks have offered settlements converting the loan into zlotys. A settlement can end the dispute, so compare it with the likely result of a court case before signing.
Deadlines

In Poland, claims by consumers are generally subject to a six-year limitation period that ends on the last day of the calendar year. For Swiss franc loans, courts have held that the period for the borrower runs from when the borrower knew, or should have known, that the clause was unfair. Deadlines in these cases are still argued in court, so do not wait: gather the loan documents and get advice early. Indicative period in Poland (contract claims): 3–6 years.

/claims/daimler-truck.t: Claims against Daimler Truck: the trucks cartel | JuriMatch
/claims/daimler-truck.d: How truck buyers claim damages from Daimler Truck for the 1997 to 2011 trucks cartel: the Commission decision, group claims and deadlines.
/claims/daimler-truck.h1: Claims against Daimler Truck: the trucks cartel
/claims/daimler-truck.lead: Daimler Truck, the German maker of Mercedes-Benz trucks, was one of the manufacturers fined by the European Commission in July 2016 for the trucks cartel. Buyers of its trucks from 1997 to 2011 have claimed damages for the overcharge, alone or in group claims.

faq.q: Can my company still claim against Daimler Truck?
faq.a: Possibly, depending on the country where you sue and when your limitation period started. After the CJEU's 2022 ruling many claims were filed, but each country's own rules decide whether yours is still open.

faq.q: Do I need the original invoices?
faq.a: They help a lot. Where they are lost, registration records and bank statements can sometimes prove the purchase and its price.

faq.q: Who pays the expert report?
faq.a: In group claims the funder or the law firm usually advances it and recovers it from the proceeds. In an individual claim, ask the firm how it is paid.

facts: Damages for overcharges

In July 2016 the European Commission found that MAN, Volvo/Renault, Daimler, Iveco and DAF had colluded for 14 years (1997 to 2011) on truck pricing and on passing on the costs of emissions technology, and in September 2017 it found the same about Scania. Buyers and lessees of medium and heavy trucks from that period have claimed the extra price they paid.
Group claims

Many hauliers have joined group claims organised by law firms, associations or claim vehicles, often backed by litigation funders, in Spain, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and elsewhere.
How the overcharge is proved

Claims rely on expert economic reports comparing cartel prices with the prices that would have applied without the cartel. Courts in several countries have estimated the damage when the evidence was incomplete.
Deadlines

In Volvo and DAF Trucks (C-267/20, June 2022) the CJEU held that the limitation period for these claims could not start before the Commission's decision was published in the EU Official Journal (April 2017 for the main decision), and applied the rules of the Damages Directive to many claims. Each country's limitation rules then apply, and some claims are already out of time. Check your dates with a lawyer before assuming your claim is open. Indicative period in Germany (non-contractual damages (tort)): 3 years (from knowledge).
